ExtraaLearn Project¶

Context¶

The EdTech industry has been surging in the past decade immensely, and according to a forecast, the Online Education market would be worth $286.62bn by 2023 with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10.26% from 2018 to 2023. The modern era of online education has enforced a lot in its growth and expansion beyond any limit. Due to having many dominant features like ease of information sharing, personalized learning experience, transparency of assessment, etc, it is now preferable to traditional education.

In the present scenario due to the Covid-19, the online education sector has witnessed rapid growth and is attracting a lot of new customers. Due to this rapid growth, many new companies have emerged in this industry. With the availability and ease of use of digital marketing resources, companies can reach out to a wider audience with their offerings. The customers who show interest in these offerings are termed as leads. There are various sources of obtaining leads for Edtech companies, like

  • The customer interacts with the marketing front on social media or other online platforms.
  • The customer browses the website/app and downloads the brochure
  • The customer connects through emails for more information.

The company then nurtures these leads and tries to convert them to paid customers. For this, the representative from the organization connects with the lead on call or through email to share further details.

Objective¶

ExtraaLearn is an initial stage startup that offers programs on cutting-edge technologies to students and professionals to help them upskill/reskill. With a large number of leads being generated on a regular basis, one of the issues faced by ExtraaLearn is to identify which of the leads are more likely to convert so that they can allocate resources accordingly. You, as a data scientist at ExtraaLearn, have been provided the leads data to:

  • Analyze and build an ML model to help identify which leads are more likely to convert to paid customers,
  • Find the factors driving the lead conversion process
  • Create a profile of the leads which are likely to convert

Data Description¶

The data contains the different attributes of leads and their interaction details with ExtraaLearn. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

Data Dictionary

  • ID: ID of the lead

  • age: Age of the lead

  • current_occupation: Current occupation of the lead. Values include 'Professional','Unemployed',and 'Student'

  • first_interaction: How did the lead first interacted with ExtraaLearn. Values include 'Website', 'Mobile App'

  • profile_completed: What percentage of profile has been filled by the lead on the website/mobile app. Values include Low - (0-50%), Medium - (50-75%), High (75-100%)

  • website_visits: How many times has a lead visited the website

  • time_spent_on_website: Total time spent on the website

  • page_views_per_visit: Average number of pages on the website viewed during the visits.

  • last_activity: Last interaction between the lead and ExtraaLearn.

    • Email Activity: Seeking for details about program through email, Representative shared information with lead like brochure of program , etc
    • Phone Activity: Had a Phone Conversation with representative, Had conversation over SMS with representative, etc
    • Website Activity: Interacted on live chat with representative, Updated profile on website, etc

  • print_media_type1: Flag indicating whether the lead had seen the ad of ExtraaLearn in the Newspaper.

  • print_media_type2: Flag indicating whether the lead had seen the ad of ExtraaLearn in the Magazine.

  • digital_media: Flag indicating whether the lead had seen the ad of ExtraaLearn on the digital platforms.

  • educational_channels: Flag indicating whether the lead had heard about ExtraaLearn in the education channels like online forums, discussion threads, educational websites, etc.

  • referral: Flag indicating whether the lead had heard about ExtraaLearn through reference.

  • status: Flag indicating whether the lead was converted to a paid customer or not.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

  • EDA is an important part of any project involving data.
  • It is important to investigate and understand the data better before building a model with it.
  • A few questions have been mentioned below which will help you approach the analysis in the right manner and generate insights from the data.
  • A thorough analysis of the data, in addition to the questions mentioned below, should be done.

Questions

  1. Leads will have different expectations from the outcome of the course and the current occupation may play a key role in getting them to participate in the program. Find out how current occupation affects lead status.
  2. The company's first impression on the customer must have an impact. Do the first channels of interaction have an impact on the lead status?
  3. The company uses multiple modes to interact with prospects. Which way of interaction works best?
  4. The company gets leads from various channels such as print media, digital media, referrals, etc. Which of these channels have the highest lead conversion rate?
  5. People browsing the website or mobile application are generally required to create a profile by sharing their personal data before they can access additional information.Does having more details about a prospect increase the chances of conversion?

Target Variable (status)

Around 29.86% of the leads were converted, while 70.14% were not converted.

This indicates a class imbalance, with non-converted leads being the majority.

Model evaluation metrics such as Recall, Precision, and F1-score will be important instead of relying only on accuracy.

Current Occupation

Majority of leads are Professionals (56.7%).

Unemployed leads represent 31.2%.

Students account for only 12%.

The dataset is dominated by working professionals, which may influence conversion patterns.

First Interaction

55.1% of leads interacted first through the Website.

44.9% came through the Mobile App.

Both channels generate a significant share of leads.

Profile Completed

Only 2.3% of leads have Low completion.

This suggests most users are engaged enough to fill out a considerable portion of their profile.

Observations:¶

Current Occupation vs Status

Professionals have the highest conversion rate (35.5%).

Unemployed leads convert at 26.6%.

Students have the lowest conversion rate (11.7%).

Occupation clearly influences conversion. Working professionals are more likely to enroll, possibly due to financial stability and career growth motivation.

First Interaction vs Status

Website leads convert at 45.6%.

Mobile App leads convert at only 10.5%.

First interaction channel has a strong impact. Website users are significantly more likely to convert than Mobile App users.

Profile Completed vs Status

High profile completion -> 41.8% conversion

Medium -> 18.9%

Low -> 7.5%

Strong positive relationship between profile completion and conversion. The more information a lead provides, the higher the probability of conversion.

This suggests engagement level is a key predictor.

Last Activity vs Status

Website Activity -> 38.5% conversion

Email Activity -> 30.3%

Phone Activity -> 21.3%

Website interactions and email follow-ups perform better than phone calls. Phone activity shows the lowest conversion rate.

Marketing Channels vs Status Print & Digital Media

Very small differences in conversion rates (~30–32%).

These channels do not show strong impact individually.

Educational Channels

Slightly lower conversion rate (27.9%) compared to non-educational leads.

Referral

Extremely high conversion rate: 67.7%

Non-referral leads convert at only 29.1%.

Referrals are the most powerful acquisition channel, even though they represent only 2% of leads.

Direct Answers to the EDA Questions¶
  1. How does current occupation affect lead status?

Yes, current occupation has a significant impact on conversion.

Professionals have the highest conversion rate (35.5%).

Unemployed leads convert at 26.6%.

Students have the lowest conversion rate (11.7%).

Conclusion: Working professionals are much more likely to convert. This may be because they:

Have higher purchasing power

Are actively seeking career advancement

See direct ROI in upskilling

Students show the lowest likelihood of conversion, possibly due to limited financial capacity.

  1. Do the first channels of interaction impact lead status?

Yes, the first interaction channel strongly impacts conversion.

Website leads convert at 45.6%.

Mobile App leads convert at only 10.5%.

Conclusion: Leads who first interact through the website are significantly more likely to convert. This suggests:

Website users may have stronger purchase intent.

Mobile App users may be more exploratory or casual visitors.

This variable appears to be a strong predictor of conversion.

  1. Which mode of interaction works best? (Last Activity)

Based on last activity:

Website Activity -> 38.5% conversion

Email Activity -> 30.3%

Phone Activity -> 21.3%

Conclusion: Website-based engagement and email communication perform better than phone calls.

Phone interactions show the lowest conversion rate, suggesting:

Cold calls may be less effective.

Digital engagement may indicate higher intent.

  1. Which acquisition channels have the highest conversion rate?

Most marketing channels (print, digital, educational) show only small differences (~30% conversion).

However:

Referral leads convert at 67.7%

Non-referral leads convert at 29.1%

Conclusion: Referrals are by far the most powerful acquisition channel, even though they represent only 2% of total leads.

This suggests:

Trust-based marketing is highly effective.

Referral programs could be expanded.

  1. Does profile completion increase the chances of conversion?

Yes — very strongly.

High completion -> 41.8% conversion

Medium -> 18.9%

Low -> 7.5%

Conclusion: There is a clear positive relationship between engagement level (profile completion) and conversion.

The more information a lead provides, the higher the probability of conversion.

This is one of the strongest predictors identified in the EDA.

                 'status']],
             hue='status')
plt.show()
Obsarvation:¶

A correlation heatmap was used to understand relationships between numerical variables. However, for categorical variables, conversion rate analysis and bar plots were more appropriate to evaluate their relationship with lead status.

In addition, a pairplot visualization was generated for the main numerical variables with the target variable as hue. This allowed a visual inspection of class separation and potential nonlinear patterns that may not be fully captured by correlation coefficients.

The correlation matrix indicates that there is no strong linear relationship among the numerical variables, as most correlation coefficients are close to zero.

The only moderately noticeable relationship is between time_spent_on_website and status (0.30), suggesting that leads who spend more time on the website are more likely to convert. This finding is also visually supported in the pairplot, where converted leads tend to show higher values for time spent compared to non-converted leads.

Age shows a weak positive correlation with status (0.12), indicating that slightly older leads may have a higher probability of converting, although the effect is limited.

Website_visits (-0.01) and page_views_per_visit (0.00) show almost no correlation with the target variable, suggesting that frequency of visits or number of pages viewed alone do not strongly influence conversion. The pairplot further confirms the lack of clear separation between classes for these variables.

Overall, the analysis suggests:

No multicollinearity concerns among numerical predictors.

No strong linear relationships between predictors.

Time_spent_on_website appears to be the most relevant numerical variable for predicting lead conversion.

Visual inspection through the pairplot reinforces that behavioral engagement (time spent) is a stronger signal than simple visit frequency.

# 1. Drop the ID column
df.drop('ID', axis=1, inplace=True)

# 2. Converting Yes/No flags to 1/0
binary_cols = ['print_media_type1', 'print_media_type2',
               'digital_media', 'educational_channels', 'referral']

for col in binary_cols:
    df[col] = df[col].apply(lambda x: 1 if x == 'Yes' else 0)

# 3. Creating Dummy Variables for categorical variables
df = pd.get_dummies(
    df,
    columns=['profile_completed',
             'current_occupation',
             'first_interaction',
             'last_activity'],
    drop_first=True
)

Data Transformation

In this section, the raw data was transformed into a machine-learning-ready format. Since most machine learning algorithms require numerical inputs, the following preprocessing steps were performed:

Column Removal

The ID column was dropped. As a unique identifier for each lead, it does not carry predictive information about the target variable (status). Keeping it could introduce noise and increase the risk of overfitting.

Binary Transformation

Several interaction flags (print_media_type1, print_media_type2, digital_media, educational_channels, and referral) were originally stored as "Yes/No" strings. These were converted into binary integers (1 for "Yes", 0 for "No") to make them suitable for numerical computation.

One-Hot Encoding (Categorical Variables)

For the categorical variables (profile_completed, current_occupation, first_interaction, and last_activity), One-Hot Encoding was applied.

Although profile_completed has an apparent ranking (Low, Medium, High), we chose not to apply ordinal encoding (0,1,2). Assigning numerical values would implicitly assume equal and linear distance between the categories, which may not reflect the true relationship with the target variable. To avoid imposing an artificial linear structure, it was treated as a categorical variable and encoded using dummy variables instead.

We used drop_first=True to remove one category from each encoded variable. This prevents multicollinearity (the dummy variable trap) and keeps the feature space more compact. While tree-based models are generally robust to correlated features, reducing redundancy improves clarity and computational efficiency.

Missing Value Treatment

Before proceeding with modeling, the dataset was examined for missing values.

A complete inspection showed that no significant missing values were present across the variables. Since there were no null entries that could bias the model or reduce statistical reliability, no imputation techniques (such as mean, median, or mode replacement) were required.

As a result, all observations were retained for further analysis and modeling.

Since Decision Tree and Random Forest models are robust to outliers and do not rely on distance-based calculations, no outlier removal or transformation was performed.

Removing these values could potentially eliminate meaningful behavioral information, particularly from highly interested leads.

The Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) was calculated to assess potential multicollinearity among the predictor variables.

Most features present VIF values close to 1, indicating very low correlation with other independent variables. This suggests that multicollinearity is not a significant concern in the dataset.

The highest VIF observed is for age (6.90). Although this value is moderately elevated, it remains below the commonly used critical threshold of 10, indicating that it does not pose a serious multicollinearity issue. Additionally, since tree-based models are not highly sensitive to multicollinearity, this value does not compromise model performance.

Other numerical variables such as page_views_per_visit (3.24) and website_visits (2.55) show mild correlation but remain within acceptable limits.

All dummy variables generated through one-hot encoding present VIF values close to 1, confirming that the use of drop_first=True successfully avoided the dummy variable trap.

Overall, the VIF analysis confirms that:

There are no severe multicollinearity issues.

The feature set is stable for modeling.

No additional feature removal is required at this stage.

Feature Scaling¶

Feature scaling was not applied to the dataset.

Tree-based models such as Decision Tree and Random Forest do not rely on distance calculations or gradient optimization. Instead, they split data based on threshold values, making them invariant to feature scaling.

Therefore, normalization or standardization was not required for this project.

Evaluation Function¶

In [19]:
# Creating metric function
def metrics_score(actual, predicted):

    print("Classification Report:\n")
    print(classification_report(actual, predicted))

    cm = confusion_matrix(actual, predicted)

    plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
    sns.heatmap(cm,
                annot=True,
                fmt='d',
                cmap='Blues',
                xticklabels=['Not Converted', 'Converted'],
                yticklabels=['Not Converted', 'Converted'])

    plt.ylabel('Actual')
    plt.xlabel('Predicted')
    plt.title('Confusion Matrix')
    plt.show()

Observations:

The metrics_score function provides a comprehensive evaluation of the classification model by combining numerical performance metrics with a visual representation through the confusion matrix.

From the classification report, we obtain:

Precision -> How reliable the model is when predicting Status = 1.

Recall -> How well the model correctly identifies actual Status = 1 cases.

F1-score -> The balance between precision and recall.

Support -> The number of observations in each Status class.

Since the primary objective is to maximize recall for the converted class (Status 1), class weights were adjusted to {0: 0.30, 1: 0.70}. This increases the penalty for misclassifying converted leads, reducing false negatives and improving the model’s ability to identify as many true conversions as possible. Prioritizing recall is essential in this context because failing to identify potential converted leads represents a greater business cost than incorrectly flagging non-converted ones.

Do we need to prune the tree?¶

Yes, pruning is necessary in this case.

The original Decision Tree achieved perfect performance on the training dataset (100% accuracy), but significantly lower performance on the test dataset (around 80%). This large gap clearly indicates overfitting.

Decision Trees are prone to overfitting when they are allowed to grow without constraints. By default, the model keeps splitting until all leaves are pure or contain very few samples, which leads to memorization of the training data rather than learning generalizable patterns.

Pruning helps by reducing the complexity of the tree and improving its ability to generalize to unseen data.

This can be achieved by tuning hyperparameters such as:

max_depth

min_samples_leaf

min_samples_split

In [25]:
# Choose the type of classifier
d_tree_tuned = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state = 7, class_weight = {0: 0.3, 1: 0.7})

# Grid of parameters to choose from
parameters = {'max_depth': np.arange(2, 10),
              'criterion': ['gini', 'entropy'],
              'min_samples_leaf': [5, 10, 20, 25]
             }

# Type of scoring used to compare parameter combinations - recall score for class 1
scorer = metrics.make_scorer(recall_score, pos_label = 1)

# Run the grid search
grid_obj = GridSearchCV(d_tree_tuned, parameters, scoring = scorer, cv = 5)

grid_obj = grid_obj.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Set the classifier to the best combination of parameters
d_tree_tuned = grid_obj.best_estimator_

# Fit the best algorithm to the data
d_tree_tuned.fit(X_train, y_train)
Out[25]:

Justification for Hyperparameter Selection

The goal of tuning the Decision Tree was to move away from the overfitted baseline model and create a classifier that generalizes well while prioritizing the identification of potential customers (Class 1).

class_weight = {0: 0.3, 1: 0.7}: This was the most critical choice. Since we have a class imbalance (70/30), we assigned a higher weight to the minority class (Status 1). This forces the model to focus on correctly predicting conversions, even if it leads to some false positives.

max_depth: np.arange(2, 10): By limiting the depth to a maximum of 9, we prevent the tree from growing too deep and "memorizing" the training data. This range explores both simple models (low variance) and more complex ones (higher detail).

min_samples_leaf: [5, 10, 20, 25]: This parameter ensures that each terminal node has a minimum number of samples. Higher values (20, 25) act as a strong regularizer, smoothing the model and preventing it from creating rules based on outliers.

scoring = scorer (Recall): Since missing a potential lead (False Negative) is more costly for ExtraaLearn than contacting a non-converter (False Positive), we optimized the grid search specifically for Recall of Class 1.

The GridSearch selected a max_depth of 3. This indicates that a very simple set of rules is enough to capture the most important patterns in lead conversion. A shallower tree is highly desirable in business because it is completely transparent and easy to explain to non-technical stakeholders.

Entropy vs. Gini: The choice of Entropy suggests that for this specific dataset, the mathematical calculation of "Information Gain" was more effective at creating pure nodes than the Gini impurity, especially when dealing with the 0.3/0.7 class weights.

Improvement in Recall:

After pruning, the model achieved a Recall of 0.89 for the converted class (Status 1) on the test set, compared to 0.63 previously. This indicates a substantial improvement in the model’s ability to identify potential converted leads, aligning with the objective of maximizing recall for class 1.

Reduced Overfitting and Better Generalization:

The Recall for class 1 is 0.91 on the training set and 0.89 on the test set, showing very consistent performance across datasets. This small gap suggests that the model is no longer overfitting significantly and is generalizing well to unseen data. The pruning process successfully reduced model complexity while maintaining strong predictive power.

Business Trade-off:

There is a decrease in Precision for class 1 (0.58 on the test set), meaning the model generates more false positives. However, this trade-off is acceptable in this context because missing a potential converted lead (false negative) represents a higher business cost than contacting a lead who ultimately does not convert.

Observations:¶

The pruned decision tree shows that first_interaction_Website is the root node, meaning it provides the highest impurity reduction in the model and therefore has the strongest initial splitting power for predicting lead conversion. This suggests that the channel of first interaction plays a critical role in influencing conversion outcomes.

On the left branch (Website as first interaction), the model predominantly predicts non-conversion (Class 0), especially for younger users and those with lower engagement signals. These nodes show very low entropy, indicating confident predictions.

On the right branch (non-Website first interaction), the tree shifts toward predicting conversion (Class 1), particularly when time spent on the website is higher and there is phone activity. Nodes such as those involving last_activity_Phone Activity demonstrate strong separation toward the converted class.

Overall, the visualization confirms that engagement-related variables (time spent, last activity, profile completion) strongly influence conversion likelihood. The pruning process keeps the tree interpretable while preserving strong separation patterns between converted and non-converted leads.

Handling Class Imbalance: Since the original data distribution is approximately 70/30 (Status 0 vs Status 1), we applied a class_weight of {0: 0.3, 1: 0.7}.

Strategy: This specific weighting tells the algorithm to treat the minority class (conversions) as significantly more important. By "penalizing" the model more for missing a conversion than for misclassifying a non-converter, we align the model with ExtraaLearn's business objective: prioritizing lead identification.

The Random Forest achieved perfect performance on the training set, with all metrics equal to 1.00 for both classes. While this may seem ideal, such results can indicate potential overfitting, since the model may have learned the training data patterns too specifically and might not generalize equally well to unseen data.

On the test set, performance was more realistic. The overall accuracy was around 0.85, indicating good general classification ability. However, since our main focus is the recall of class 1, it is important to highlight that it was approximately 0.73. This means that about 73% of the actual class 1 instances were correctly identified, while roughly 27% were misclassified as class 0.

This is particularly important if class 1 represents the critical outcome in the problem (such as fraud, churn, or a risk condition), because a recall of 0.73 implies a noticeable number of false negatives. Therefore, even though the overall performance is solid, it may be beneficial to further tune the model to improve recall for class 1 if reducing false negatives is the primary objective.

Observations:¶

Balanced Predictive Power: Unlike the single Decision Tree, the Random Forest shows a more distributed importance across features. This indicates a more robust model that considers multiple signals before making a prediction.

Top Conversion Drivers: Time spent on website (27.3%) and First interaction via Website (18.8%) remain the most critical predictors. This reinforces that digital engagement and the initial touchpoint are the strongest indicators of lead intent.

The Role of Demographics and Browsing Behavior: Interestingly, features like Page views per visit (10.9%), Profile completion - Medium (10.7%), and Age (10.3%) now show significant importance (all above 10%). This suggests that the lead's profile and their specific browsing patterns provide essential context that the simpler model might have overlooked.

Lower-Impact Features: Features like website_visits and last_activity contribute moderately, while marketing flags (media types and referrals) remain at the bottom of the list. This suggests that while acquisition channels bring leads in, their behavioral data after joining the platform is what truly determines conversion.

Do we need to prune the tree?¶

Yes. Even though a Random Forest is naturally more robust than a single Decision Tree, The model achieved 100% across all metrics on the training set. This is the definition of "memorization" (overfitting). By "pruning" the forest, which we do by tuning hyperparameters like max_depth and min_samples_leaf forcing the model to focus on the strongest patterns that actually generalize to new leads, rather than noise in the training data.

In [35]:
# Choose the type of classifier
rf_estimator_tuned = RandomForestClassifier(criterion = "entropy", random_state = 7)

# Grid of parameters to choose from
parameters = {
    "n_estimators": [100, 150],
    "max_depth": [3, 5, 7],
    "min_samples_leaf": [20, 30],
    "max_features": ["sqrt", 0.8],
    "class_weight": ["balanced", {0: 0.3, 1: 0.7}]
}

# Type of scoring used to compare parameter combinations - recall score for class 1
scorer = metrics.make_scorer(recall_score, pos_label = 1)

# Run the grid search on the training data using scorer=scorer and cv=5
grid_obj = GridSearchCV(rf_estimator_tuned, parameters, scoring = scorer, cv = 5)

# Fit the grid search to the training data
grid_obj = grid_obj.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Save the best estimator to variable rf_estimator_tuned
rf_estimator_tuned = grid_obj.best_estimator_

RandomForestClassifier(class_weight='balanced', criterion='entropy',
                       max_depth=3, max_features=0.8, min_samples_leaf=20,
                       random_state=7)
Observations:¶

Justification for Hyperparameter Selection (Random Forest)

n_estimators [100, 150]: We chose a solid range of trees to stabilize the predictions. Increasing the number of estimators helps reduce the model's variance, ensuring that the final lead classification is the result of a robust consensus across the forest.

max_depth [3, 5, 7]: Following the insight from the Tuned Decision Tree—where a depth of 3 was found to be optimal—we included lower depth values. This forces the forest to focus on high-level, statistically significant features rather than over-complicating the decision boundaries.

min_samples_leaf [20, 30]: Based on the Decision Tree results where a min_samples_leaf of 5 was effective for a single tree, we tested higher values (20, 30) for the Random Forest. This serves as a stronger regularizer for an ensemble, ensuring that the aggregated nodes across 100+ trees are based on large, stable clusters of data rather than noise. (As demonstrated in the "Technical Appendix" at the end of this notebook, a separate test was conducted comparing values 5 and 20, and the results remained identical.)

max_features ["sqrt", 0.8]: We compared the standard square root (approx. 4 features) against a more aggressive 80% feature set. This allows the GridSearchCV to decide if the forest performs better by forcing diversity between trees or by allowing each tree to have a nearly complete view of the key drivers (like Time Spent on Website).

class_weight ["balanced", {0: 0.3, 1: 0.7}]: Given the 70/30 class imbalance, we tested the 'balanced' mode against a custom weight. This is critical for driving the Recall higher, as it specifically penalizes the model more for missing a potential converter (Status 1).

Convergent Performance (Recall Focus): Both models have now converged to a very similar performance profile after tuning. Both prioritized Recall (0.89), successfully identifying 89% of potential converters. This indicates that the tuning process successfully pushed both models to their maximum potential for capturing leads.

Precision and F1-Score Stability: The Tuned Random Forest shows a slightly better F1-Score (0.71 vs 0.70) on the test set compared to the Decision Tree. While the Precision is identical (0.58), the Random Forest's ensemble nature provides a marginal edge in the balance between capturing leads and maintaining overall model health.

Exceptional Generalization: Both models demonstrate nearly perfect generalization. The drop in accuracy from Training (0.79) to Test (0.78) is negligible. This confirms that the constraints applied, specifically the max_depth of 3 and min_samples_leaf, successfully eliminated the overfitting seen in the baseline models.

The Power of Simplicity: It is noteworthy that both the single tree and the forest achieved their best results with a max_depth of 3. This proves that the conversion logic for ExtraaLearn leads is driven by a few highly influential features rather than a complex web of variables."

Observations:¶

The feature importance analysis reveals a highly concentrated decision-making process, where a few key drivers dictate the vast majority of the model's predictive power.

The "Golden Duo" of Engagement: time_spent_on_website (37.1%) and first_interaction_Website (35.2%) are, by far, the most influential predictors. Together, they account for over 72% of the model's logic. This confirms that leads who spend significant time on the site and choose the website as their initial touchpoint are the most likely to convert.

The Quality Indicator: profile_completed_Medium (17.9%) stands as the third pillar of the model. This highlights that the intent to provide more detailed information during the sign-up process is a strong behavioral signal of high-intent customers.

Marginal Impact of Demographic/Passive Data: Interestingly, variables like age (2.7%), current_occupation, and page_views_per_visit have very low importance. This suggests that what the lead does (behavioral data) is significantly more predictive than who the lead is (demographic data).

Redundant Channels: Several features, such as digital_media, educational_channels, and referral, show 0% importance. This indicates that these channels do not contribute to the final conversion decision in the presence of more dominant features, allowing for potential simplification of future data collection.

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

Actionable Insights and Recommendations Following the Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), class imbalance handling, and the fine-tuning of Machine Learning models, we have identified the critical drivers that transform a lead into a customer.

1 Key Business Insights The Power of the First Impression: Leads whose first interaction occurs via the Website have a significantly higher probability of conversion. The website is not just a storefront; it is the primary filter for lead quality.

Time is Gold: Time spent on the website emerged as the most important variable. There is a definitive "tipping point" where digital engagement translates into real purchase intent.

Profile Completion Matters: Leads with profiles categorized as "Medium" or "High" show superior conversion rates. A lead's willingness to provide information directly correlates with their propensity to enroll.

The Recall Priority: By prioritizing a Recall of 0.89, ExtraaLearn ensures that nearly 9 out of every 10 potential students are identified. This minimizes the opportunity cost of losing a customer to the competition.

2 Strategic Recommendations Optimize Digital Marketing Spend Action: Reallocate the paid media budget toward channels that drive users directly to the Official Website, rather than external forms or third-party landing pages.

Goal: Maximize the volume of leads starting their journey through the highest-converting channel.

Implement a High-Engagement "Fast Track" Action: Set up real-time CRM alerts for the sales team whenever a lead exceeds the average engagement time threshold identified by the model.

Goal: Approach the lead while their interest is at its peak ("strike while the iron is hot").

Gamify Profile Completion Action: Introduce progress bars or small incentives (e.g., free e-books or trial access) for leads with "Low" profiles to complete their data.

Goal: Move leads from "Low" to "Medium/High" categories, increasing the pool of qualified leads for the model.

Sales Resource Allocation Action: Use the Random Forest probability scores to distribute leads. High-probability leads should be assigned to senior consultants, while lower-probability leads can be nurtured via automated email campaigns.

3 Final Recommendation The Tuned Random Forest is recommended as the final production model. While it provides the same high Recall (0.89) as the Tuned Decision Tree, its ensemble architecture offers greater long-term stability and robustness. This model ensures that ExtraaLearn maximizes its revenue by capturing the vast majority of potential leads while maintaining a consistent and reliable scoring mechanism for the sales team.

Technical Appendix¶

The following test was conducted to evaluate the sensitivity and robustness of the Random Forest model regarding its leaf granularity. By keeping the optimal max_depth of 3 and class_weight as 'balanced', we compared the model’s performance using min_samples_leaf values of 5 (the optimal value for the single Decision Tree) and 20 (the initial choice for the Forest ensemble). The goal was to determine if a more granular leaf structure would yield any gains in Recall or Precision, or if the model’s performance had already reached a state of stability where such micro-adjustments no longer impact the final classification of leads.

After performing a separate sensitivity test, it was observed that the model's performance metrics remained exactly the same when comparing min_samples_leaf values of 5 and 20. This result confirms that the primary patterns in the ExtraaLearn dataset are captured by the broader tree structure (defined by the max_depth of 3) rather than the granularity of individual leaf nodes. The fact that the Precision (0.58) and Recall (0.89) did not fluctuate proves that the model has reached a peak state of stability, where it is no longer sensitive to minor parameter adjustments. This provides high confidence that the chosen configuration is robust and will perform consistently when applied to new, unseen leads.

Examples
--------

    The simplest way to use nbconvert is

            > jupyter nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --to html

            Options include ['asciidoc', 'custom', 'html', 'latex', 'markdown', 'notebook', 'pdf', 'python', 'qtpdf', 'qtpng', 'rst', 'script', 'slides', 'webpdf'].

            > jupyter nbconvert --to latex mynotebook.ipynb

            Both HTML and LaTeX support multiple output templates. LaTeX includes
            'base', 'article' and 'report'.  HTML includes 'basic', 'lab' and
            'classic'. You can specify the flavor of the format used.

            > jupyter nbconvert --to html --template lab mynotebook.ipynb

            You can also pipe the output to stdout, rather than a file

            > jupyter nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --stdout

            PDF is generated via latex

            > jupyter nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --to pdf

            You can get (and serve) a Reveal.js-powered slideshow

            > jupyter nbconvert myslides.ipynb --to slides --post serve

            Multiple notebooks can be given at the command line in a couple of
            different ways:

            > jupyter nbconvert notebook*.ipynb
            > jupyter nbconvert notebook1.ipynb notebook2.ipynb

            or you can specify the notebooks list in a config file, containing::

                c.NbConvertApp.notebooks = ["my_notebook.ipynb"]

            > jupyter nbconvert --config mycfg.py

To see all available configurables, use `--help-all`.
